section_summary: This section documents mounting public and congressional pressure to halt American exports of scrap iron, machinery, petroleum, arms, and other materials to Japan during the war in China. It includes petitions, constituent letters, proposed legislation, State Department replies explaining the limits of the Neutrality Act, and an internal analysis disputing the claim that the United States supplied 54 percent of all Japanese war materials. The section concludes with a substantial excerpt from the State Department’s 1938 regulations governing international traffic in arms.

subfiles.title: Petition protesting shipments of scrap iron and war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Residents of San Diego County, California
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Petitioners protest the shipment of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These pages continue a printed petition circulated by the Peace Committee of San Diego. The forms contain numerous handwritten signatures and addresses, many of which are badly degraded in the OCR, from San Diego, Julian, Lakeside, and nearby communities.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting peace and refugee appeals
subfiles.from: Mr. Powell, Associate Professor at Smith College
subfiles.about: A Smith College professor forwards appeals for Hull’s consideration and expresses confidence in his judgment.
subfiles.summary: Writer asks Hull to consider enclosed peace and refugee appeals, with a personal note recalling Hull's wife introducing him to his wife at Rockbridge Alum Springs.

subfiles.title: American Committee appeal to Mr. and Mrs. Powell
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The committee solicits money for a national campaign against American supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Committee appeal to the Powells: American scrap iron, oil and trucks sustain Japan's aggression; it seeks contributions to a $50,000 publicity campaign for legislation.

subfiles.title: Northampton Committee appeal for refugee children
subfiles.about: The circular urges immediate lobbying to admit more German refugee children to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Northampton Committee appeals for German refugee children, noting Ireland, England and France have admitted many, and urges using German immigration quotas.

subfiles.title: FBI notice of Mobile scrap-iron advertisement
subfiles.about: Hoover reports an advertisement seeking junk and scrap iron for Japan.
subfiles.summary: FBI forwards a notice of a January 15 Mobile Register scrap-iron advertisement by the Marine Junk Company, noting no Bureau investigation.

subfiles.title: San Diego peace groups’ letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Kate H. Newing for San Diego peace organizations
subfiles.about: San Diego peace activists ask Roosevelt to encourage legislation fulfilling American moral obligations concerning Japan.
subfiles.summary: San Diego peace groups send Roosevelt a copy of their State Department letter and renew the request for legislation on the nation's moral responsibility.

subfiles.title: Copy of San Diego petition-transmittal letter
subfiles.from: Kate H. Newing and associated San Diego peace groups
subfiles.about: The writer forwards 1,001 signatures protesting shipments of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Copy of a San Diego letter enclosing 1,001 protest signatures and urging a practical policy to counteract Japanese action in China.

subfiles.title: Capper letter forwarding an Ottawa church protest
subfiles.about: Senator Capper forwards a Kansas church protest and asks why scrap-iron exports remain legal under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Senator Capper forwards an Ottawa church protest like many from Kansas, urges ending scrap-iron shipments to any warring nation, and asks Hull to explain the legal position.

subfiles.title: First Christian Church protest against war supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Members of the First Christian Church, Ottawa, Kansas
subfiles.about: Church members ask Capper to stop all American shipments of manufactured or raw war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The signers contend that supplying Japan is inconsistent with the United States’ claim to be a Christian nation. They argue that ending such shipments could help stop the slaughter of Chinese people; the second page contains additional, poorly legible signatures.

subfiles.title: Hull explanation of the Neutrality Act and scrap iron
subfiles.about: Hull explains why existing neutrality legislation does not authorize an embargo on scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains the Neutrality Act covers only arms and implements of war, not scrap iron; invoking it would bar arms to China too, and licensed exports since July 1937 were larger to China than to Japan.

subfiles.title: Handwritten appeal concerning China and refugee children
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull or the Department of State
subfiles.about: The writer urges policies assisting China and increasing admission of refugee children.
subfiles.summary: Although much of the handwriting is illegible, the letter expresses hope that cutting supplies or otherwise weakening Japan would help China. It also asks for support of reasonable proposals to admit more refugee children from difficult and pressing circumstances.

subfiles.title: McCormack letter forwarding the Kings’ protest
subfiles.about: McCormack forwards a Massachusetts constituent letter protesting war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative McCormack forwards a protest from John and Estelle King of Mattapan for the Department's information.

subfiles.title: John and Estelle King protest to McCormack
subfiles.from: John G. King and Estelle H. King
subfiles.about: The Kings urge McCormack to support legislation ending war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Kings protest continued American war-material exports to Japan as shameful and ask McCormack to support legislation to stop them.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to McCormack
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the Kings’ protest and says their views have been noted.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges the Kings' January 22 letter via McCormack, saying only that their views have been recorded.

subfiles.title: Request for State Department report on H.R. 3419
subfiles.about: The House Foreign Affairs chairman requests a report on a bill restricting iron and steel exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: McReynolds sends H.R. 3419, which would prohibit exports of pig iron, scrap iron and scrap steel to China and Japan for military use, and requests a State Department report.

subfiles.title: H.R. 3419: bill prohibiting iron and steel exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: The bill proposes criminal penalties for exporting pig iron, scrap iron, or scrap steel for military use in China or Japan.
subfiles.summary: H.R. 3419 would prohibit direct exports, and exports routed through other ports, of specified iron and steel products intended for military purposes in China or Japan. Each unlawful shipment would be a separate misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $5,000 or imprisonment for up to one year.

subfiles.title: Hull request for Budget Bureau clearance of H.R. 3419 report
subfiles.about: Hull asks whether the proposed departmental report on H.R. 3419 accords with the President’s program.
subfiles.summary: Hull asks the Budget Bureau whether the proposed report on H.R. 3419 for the House Foreign Affairs Committee is consistent with the President's program.

subfiles.title: Interim acknowledgment concerning H.R. 3419
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the request for a report on H.R. 3419 and promises a later response.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges McReynolds's request on H.R. 3419, saying a report will follow shortly.

subfiles.title: State Department report recommending postponement of H.R. 3419
subfiles.about: Hull recommends postponing H.R. 3419 until Congress considers neutrality policy comprehensively.
subfiles.summary: Hull reports that the proposed export ban is part of broader neutrality policy and suggests the committee defer H.R. 3419 until Congress examines neutrality policy fully.

subfiles.title: Church inquiry about alleged arms shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Church asks whether constituent claims about arms and ammunition shipments to Japan are factual and how such exports could be stopped.
subfiles.summary: Ralph Church, receiving many protests, asks for information on the alleged trade and the steps needed to prevent it.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Ralph E. Church
subfiles.about: Hull supplies copies of a departmental statement on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends Church ten copies of a State Department statement on arms exports to Japan for answering constituents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for cargo aboard the Sintoku Maru
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers to a Commerce Department letter about cargo shipped from Hilo to Kobe aboard a Japanese training ship.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference on the Japanese government training ship Sintoku Maru's cargo of rubber, metal and merchandise, with a January 4 Honolulu customs communication.

subfiles.title: Rees acknowledgment of State Department position
subfiles.about: Rees thanks Hull for explaining his position on preventing scrap-iron and steel exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rees briefly acknowledges Hull's reply on restricting iron and steel scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Provenance of Materials Used by Japan in the Conduct of the Conflict in China
subfiles.doc_type: State Department memorandum with statistical annex
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates the claim that the United States supplied 54 percent of the materials used by Japan in China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that the widely quoted 54.4 percent figure concerns Japan’s 1937 imports of thirteen selected commodities, not its total supply or actual military consumption. It emphasizes omitted factors such as Japanese domestic production, stocks accumulated before the war, and supplies originating in or entering Manchuria and occupied Chinese territory. The analysis concludes that the true American share of Japan’s total war-material supply was probably far below 54 percent, while acknowledging heavy Japanese dependence on the United States for petroleum, iron, and copper. An annex tabulates shortages, foreign sources, requirements, and domestic production for twenty-nine strategic commodities or commodity groups.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Vermont resolution
subfiles.about: The White House refers correspondence concerning a Vermont resolution on war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: White House routing sheet from McIntyre, February 6, 1939, transmitting Vermont materials to State for action.

subfiles.title: Vermont secretary’s transmittal of J.R.H. 10
subfiles.from: Rawson C. Myrick, Secretary of State of Vermont
subfiles.about: The Vermont secretary of state sends the President a certified copy of a joint resolution on war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vermont's secretary Myrick transmits J.R.H. 10, a joint resolution on shipping war materials to Japan, approved January 27, 1939.

subfiles.title: Vermont Joint Resolution Relating to the Shipment of War Materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Vermont Senate and House of Representatives
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States and the Vermont congressional delegation
subfiles.about: Vermont calls for immediate governmental pressure to prohibit sales and shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vermont joint resolution says Japan gets over half its war commodities from American manufacturers and urges every governmental agency to pressure an end to the trade; copy certified February 2, 1939.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Vermont resolution
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges the certified Vermont resolution and provides information about arms exports.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Vermont for sending the resolution to the President, promises careful consideration, and encloses a statement on arms exports to Japan and China.

subfiles.title: Lex Green letter forwarding the Penney Farms petition
subfiles.about: Green forwards a petition from James S. Jewell and other residents of Penney Farms, Florida.
subfiles.summary: Lex Green forwards a Penney Farms petition, signed by many residents, to Hull for information.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Lex Green concerning the Penney Farms petition
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the petition and supplies a departmental statement for possible transmission to James S. Jewell.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that the petition’s information about exports of war materials to Japan has been carefully noted. He encloses a statement on exports of arms, ammunition, and implements of war to Japan and China and returns the original petition.

subfiles.title: Budget Bureau clearance of report on H.R. 3419
subfiles.from: Executive Assistant, Bureau of the Budget
subfiles.about: The Budget Bureau approves submission of the State Department’s proposed report recommending postponement of H.R. 3419.
subfiles.summary: Budget Bureau returns the proposed H.R. 3419 report, raising no objection to postponing consideration pending a comprehensive neutrality review.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Peabody’s appeal for action against supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Peabody presses Hull to end American material support for Japan and aid China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Peabody says concern in Florida extends to businesspeople, rejects the claim neutrality measures are unavailable without a declaration of war, and urges immediate action, enclosing an American Committee appeal.

subfiles.title: American Committee appeal to Mrs. Peabody
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The committee requests financial support for a national campaign to stop American war supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Committee fundraising appeal to Mrs. Peabody, substantially the same as the Powell appeal, for a $50,000 legislative campaign.

subfiles.title: Moore reply to Mrs. Peabody
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges Peabody’s views but declines to add to earlier State Department replies.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Mrs. Peabody, refers her to May 31 and September 9, 1938 letters, and assures continued study.

subfiles.title: Export statistics for machinery and metals sent to Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Commerce Department figures for machine tools, refined copper, and scrap brass and bronze exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum with annual figures on machine-tool, refined copper and scrap exports to Japan; quoting them in the reply to Thompson would serve no purpose.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter about machinery shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Thompson alleges that automatic machinery useful for producing munitions and aircraft parts is being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thompson praises Hull's speech but says automatic manufacturing machinery capable of stamping munitions or aircraft parts is still exported to Japan.

subfiles.title: International Traffic in Arms: Laws and Regulations Administered by the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Manufacturers, importers, exporters, and the public
subfiles.about: The pamphlet sets out federal laws, proclamations, registration requirements, and licensing rules governing international trade in arms and implements of war.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt reproduces section 5 of the 1937 neutrality joint resolution, Roosevelt’s May 1, 1937 proclamation defining seven categories of controlled arms and munitions, and detailed State Department regulations for registration and shipment licensing. It includes model applications and certificates, exemptions, customs procedures, recordkeeping rules, and provisions protecting military secrets. The final pages begin special rules governing exports to China, Cuba, Honduras, and Nicaragua, including the 1922 statutory authority and related inter-American convention; the pamphlet continues beyond this section.
